cat > /tmp/pr-body.md <<'MDEOF'
The Paper file's five console screens, and the API work they needed. Six
commits, each one landing its own lanes, gates, and doc rows.

## The counter route could never answer

`crates/cachet-worker/src/api.rs:142` reads
`env.var("CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID")` on every request and the alchemy
program never bound it, so `GET /api/self/events` answered 503
`storage_unavailable` on every deployment, including one configured with
a stats token. The counting worked; the reporting had not run once since
the route shipped in #24.

Nobody noticed because the route's success path had no test coverage of
any kind. `workerd/wrangler.toml` bound no Analytics Engine dataset and
set no token, so all six lane rows were refused at the config check
before any query ran, and `stats::emit` returned early in every scenario.
`run_stats_sql`, the row deserialization, the response shaping, and the
whole writer path were untested.

Both halves are fixed. `loadStageConfig` now refuses a stats token that
arrives without an account id, because half a credential is a chart that
never loads rather than an error anyone sees. The lane's stub server
gained a fourth role, Cloudflare's SQL API, reached through a new
`CACHET_STATS_API_URL` seam the way the JWKS and GitHub API are already
reached through theirs. It receives the composed statement as text, so
the lane asserts it whole rather than by substring: this statement runs
with an account token behind it.

## What the screens needed

`by=hour` and `by=day` group into time buckets and answer a series:
oldest first, one row per bucket, zeros included, each dimension the
bucket's first instant in epoch seconds. A bucket finer than its window
can hold is refused rather than truncated, because a truncated series is
a chart that silently starts partway through its own window. `kind`,
`outcome`, and `actor` narrow an answer to one value each, which is what
makes "laptop reads by outcome" askable.

Filters meant the writer's vocabulary had to close: `StatKind` and
`StatOutcome` replace the free strings, so a filter value parses into the
same set the writers emit before anything is formatted into SQL. One test
now ties the two sides together where a comment used to name the risk.

Three more things that surfaced on the way. Writes never measured their
bytes, so "pushed this week" had no source. The multipart open and
completion branches returned past the counter, so `begin` and `complete`
were kinds the router named and no point ever carried. And `by=project`
could only ever answer one empty row, because nothing had ever filled
`blob6`.

`GET /api/whoami` answers who a request authenticates as, admin or not: a
console that could only learn its standing by provoking a 403 would make
a refusal part of loading a page. `GET /api/self/health` answers the
console header's status and countdown.

## A browser session could read the cache

`read_routes` authorized narinfo and NAR reads through `authorize_read`,
which accepts the session cookie and answers `ReadIdentity::Session` with
no scope attached. `resolve_session` never re-checks org membership, so a
copy of an ex-member's cookie substituted from the cache for up to a
fortnight after they left.

Sessions are see-only now: they authenticate the console's own surface
and answer 401 on the paths that serve cache bytes. Nix reads through a
netrc and never sends a cookie, so nothing that reads for real loses a
credential. ADR 0016 records the scope and names the fourteen-day counter
window as an accepted trade rather than leaving the threat model claiming
a re-check the code never performed.

## Serving the console

Assets mount under `/console` on the worker's own deployment, and the
root redirects there. Same origin is what makes the session cookie work
at all: it is `SameSite=Lax` on `Path=/`, and the worker emits no
`Access-Control-*` headers.

Both of the asset layer's handling modes are off, and that is the whole
safety argument. A binary cache is read by asking about paths that mostly
are not in it, and nix reads a 404 as "ask the next substituter". A layer
answering an unmatched request with an application shell turns every
cache miss into `200 text/html`.

`run_worker_first: true` was the first answer and it was wrong: it puts
the worker in front of `/cdn-cgi/*`, which the platform and the local
runner reserve, and it broke the collector's dev endpoint immediately.
ADR 0014 records that.

## The console

Five screens: what the cache holds and what pushed it, what the collector
has been doing, who can reach the deployment, the traffic it serves, and
what it does for people rather than for CI. It reads and never writes.

React with TanStack Router and Query, StyleX against the tokens carried
over from the design, and hand-drawn SVG for the charts. Every answer
decodes through an `effect` schema before a screen sees it, so a
deployment newer or older than the console beside it fails at the
boundary with the field named rather than three components later as an
`undefined` on screen.

The states the mockups do not draw are the ones a real deployment
reaches, and each says what is true instead of showing an error: signed
out, an org member who is not an admin, a deployment that has never
collected, and one counting without a token to report with.

## Two bugs found by running it rather than by testing it

StyleX compiles longhands, so `background: "none"` was dropped and every
button fell back to the user agent's light default. And the bars' track
and fill were spans, which are inline, so neither the height nor the
width applied and every row rendered as the same full-width strip.

## A lane bug, not a flake

The push payload was `cachet workerd lane payload <pid>`, and the
operating system recycles pids. A run that drew one an earlier run had
already pushed found its path in the store snapshot, uploaded nothing,
minted no token, and failed three checks at once with nothing in any
message to say why. Three such paths were sitting in a dev machine's
store. The content is a uuid now, and the mint assertions carry the count
they actually saw.

Two more caught by tests rather than by luck: the property lane found an
epoch boundary where the series window ran off the front and ended in the
future, and the console's schema test caught a mirror in `cachet-api`
carrying `skip_serializing_if` on a field the core type writes as `null`,
so the generated document promised an absent key for one that is always
present. That mirror test now compares serializations rather than fields.

## Gates

A new lane, `console`, with its row in `lanes.toml`, its doc, its verb,
and its CI job. `just check` passes, the workerd lane is green with a new
scenario for the console's routing law, and the integration lane gains
three steps: the root redirects, the shell serves and names a script the
build emitted, and an absent narinfo still answers 404 and not HTML.

ADRs 0014, 0015, and 0016. `docs/console.md` joins the §11 manifest.

content.text:
No, and both of its settings are now traps.

**As an override** (`CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN=https://ui.example.com`) it redirects the browser to a UI that structurally cannot authenticate. The session cookie is `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` on the deployment's host, the worker emits no `Access-Control-*` headers, and it answers `OPTIONS` with a 404. So the person lands on that origin with no credential and no way to acquire one. The redirect works; nothing after it does.

**As an off switch** (`CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN=""`) it answers 204 instead of redirecting, but it doesn't disable anything. No. Creating the environment changes nothing about the automatic path.

The `workflow_run` trigger only ever reaches the `staging` job, and that job is doubly hardcoded: `environment: staging` on line 36, `just deploy cachet-staging` on line 66. Neither reads `inputs.stage`, because on a `workflow_run` event there are no inputs. Production can only be reached through `manual` (line 99), which is gated on `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'` — a button press.

So creating a `production` environment does exactly one thing: makes the dispatch path work instead of failing at config load. And if you put a required-reviewer rule on it, the dispatched run parks and waits for your approval before any step executes, which is the gate DEPLOY.md describes.

Worth knowing about the concurrency group on line 27: it keys on `inputs.stage` for a dispatch and `cachet-staging` otherwise, so a production deploy and a staging deploy occupy different slots and never queue behind each other.

The one sharp edge is that `manual` accepts `cachet-staging` too, and then resolves to the `staging` environment — so the same environment's secrets serve both a hand-triggered staging deploy and the automatic one. That's deliberate and fine; it just means production is the only stage whose secrets would live somewhere new.

All seven pushed as `a8515ff`, signed. Staging redeploys on green `ci`.

**The basic-auth prompt** was the worker sending `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` on *every* 401, including `/api/whoami`, which the console fetches on load. Browsers open their native credential dialog for that header even on a `fetch`, so you got a password box before the sign-in screen could render. **Case folding** was a real fail-closed bug: a correct admins list that refuses its admin. Logins, org slugs, repository names, and project names all fold on ingest, so no comparison downstream is case-sensitive. Worth knowing — project names becoming bucket keys means a lease stored under a mixed-case key is unreachable after this and gets swept after grace, then recreated on the next push. Every name in this deployment is already lowercase, so it's a no-op here.

**The mark** was nothing like the design. It's the capacitor now: `M2 12 H9 M15 12 H22 M9 5 V19 M15 5 V19`, straight from the Paper node.

**The clock** measured 720 on a 1440 viewport — dead centre. It was `space-between` on three flex children, so it was only ever centred by coincidence and drifted entirely when the right-hand group was empty, which it is for anyone who isn't an admin.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.246/887ca369e7736125f5679cd18b3d5a53/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

result.output:
# Interaction - tooltips & filters

An HTML chart is interactive by default - the hover layer is part of the deliverable,
not an upgrade. Omitting it is the exception (a bare stat tile), never the default.
Design it with the same care as the static render.

## Tooltips & hover

Tooltips **enhance, they never gate**: every value a tooltip shows is also reachable
without it, through direct labels or the table view. Same details on keyboard focus
as on hover.

- **The crosshair finds the X.** A vertical hairline tracks the pointer and snaps to
  the nearest data position. Readers aim at a date, never at a 2px line.
- **On bars and cells, the mark is the hit target.** No crosshair - each bar, segment,
  dot, or heat-cell carries its own `pointermove`/`focus` tooltip showing category and
  value, and the hovered mark lifts (slight lighten or outline) so the reader sees it respond.
- **One tooltip, every series.** The readout lists every series at that X - the
  pointer never has to land on a line or a fill to get a value.
- **Labels are untrusted data - use `textContent`.** Series and category names
  often come from CSV headers, tool output, or API responses. Insert them into
  tooltip/legend/table DOM with `textContent` or `createTextNode`, never via
  `innerHTML` string concatenation.
- **Values lead, labels follow.** In the tooltip the value is the Strong,
  high-contrast element and the series name is secondary - the legend's hierarchy
  inverted, because here the reader has the series and wants the number.
- **Line keys, not boxes.** Tooltip rows key their series with a short stroke of the
  series color; at tooltip density a filled box is data-weight ink doing a label's
  job. (Legends still mirror the mark: rect for bars/areas, line for lines.)
- **The hit target is bigger than the mark.** A mark's hover/focus area includes its
  2px surface gap and then some - never only the painted pixels. An 8px scatter dot is a
  pinpoint nobody hits reliably; give each point a transparent hit area of at least
  **24px**, or - for dense scatter - a nearest-point / Voronoi layer so the pointer only
  has to be *closest*, not dead-center. (The crosshair already does this for the X on
  line and bar charts; scatter and bubble need the per-point version.)
- **A value pushed off its mark lives in the tooltip.** When a label won't fit inside a
  small bar (see `marks-and-anatomy.md`), that bar's hit area carries the value on hover
  and focus - the tooltip is its overflow home, and the table view keeps it reachable
  without hovering at all.

## Filters & time ranges

Every monitoring dashboard needs the same controls. These are **standard UI, not
chart marks** - build them with ordinary HTML form controls styled to match the
chart chrome. Dataviz only adds composition rules:

- **One row, above the charts.** Filters sit in a single left-aligned row above the
  content they scope - never inside a chart card, never per-chart. If one chart needs
  its own range, it's a different dashboard.
- **Date range first.** It's the filter every reader reaches for; presets (today,
  last 7 / 30 / 90 days) before a custom range.
- **Filters scope everything below them.** Every chart, stat, and table re-renders
  against the same slice, so the numbers always agree.
- **Refetch keeps the frame.** While data reloads, charts hold their previous render
  at reduced opacity - no skeleton, no layout jump, no flash.

A good date picker lists presets as rows (nobody fights a calendar grid for "last 30
days"), marks selection with a 16px bold check, keeps hover a ghost wash so it never
competes with selection, and tucks the custom range behind a hairline in the footer.
(See `palette.md` for the reference spec.)

Pushed as `6938108`. Everything you flagged is in, and I verified each in the browser rather than assuming:

| | |
|---|---|
| Basic-auth prompt | Challenge confined to nix object paths; lane asserts both sides |
| Lowercase | Logins, orgs, repos, project names fold on ingest |

content.text:
Pushed as `284e200`.

**On why you kept seeing that prose after I said I'd deleted it:** my earlier edits were exact-string replacements, `nix fmt` had rewrapped those paragraphs since I wrote them, so the matches failed and did nothing — and I didn't assert on the replacements, so it looked like success. This pass matched structurally and asserted the count on every one. That's on me; you shouldn't have had to report the same text three times.

Gone now: the laptop-token paragraph, the who-pushes paragraph, the what-a-gate-is paragraph, the `cachet doctor` instructions, and the "You signed in through GitHub as…" sentence. Also cut "Set in the deploy config" and "Tokens last thirty days" — headings describing where a value came from rather than what it is.

The session expiry is in the status bar now: `Signed in as shivansh (admin) · expires 8 Sep 2026 · pkg-cache.loopholelabs.io`.

Table columns share the width instead of bunching left, and RESULT is just `Completed` or `Stopped` — the gate name is in the detail panel, which is already scoped to one run.

What's left as prose is only the empty-state notes (`no collection has finished yet`, `counts and cannot report`, `this screen is for admins`) and short factual lines like `Nothing was pushed this week`. Say the word if any of those should go too.
Node IDs: 7L6-0 <- what else do we need from that header? Should we have those things? Is it worth the complication?

That's a different product's HUD (`SESAME 0.4.2`, `NOX.SO`). Going through it against what cachet can answer truthfully:

**Already covered.** `NOX.SO` + build sha → cachet's strip already reads `CACHET · PRODUCTION · V1.2.0 · A4F31C`. `● NOMINAL` → `● HEALTHY`, which is derived from the last collection rather than asserted.

**Can't answer honestly.** `T+ 0128` uptime is meaningless for a Worker — isolates start and die per request, so there's no process to have been up. `LAST DEPLOY 4M AGO` would need a second build stamp, and the sha already answers the question it's a proxy for ("is this the build I shipped").

**Would actively mislead.** `EDGE · SJC` is available (`request.cf.colo`), but on the console it's the colo that served *the console's own* request. A reader would take it as where their builds are served from, and it isn't. If colo mattered it'd belong as a counter dimension, and the dataset doesn't record one.

**The one real gap: `P50 41 MS · P95 88`.** cachet records no durations at all — `StatPoint` carries count and bytes and nothing else. Latency would mean a third double on every point, a quantile query shape, its lane rows, and a DEPLOY.md column row. Analytics Engine can do quantiles, so it's buildable. But it's a chart on Traffic, not a number in a strip — a p95 with no distribution behind it is a number you can't act on.

So: **nothing from that header is worth adding to the HUD.** The strip's job is telling you which deployment you're looking at and whether its collector is keeping up, and it does both. Latency is worth building when you want it, as its own thing on Traffic, and it's maybe a day of work across the writer, the query surface, the lane, and the docs.

Want me to open an issue for the latency work so it's written down, or leave it?

I think we probably want to put the word COMMIT before the commit hash. I think the EDGE SJC bit isn't a lie because the user's nix cache requests will be also served from the same nearby worker. The latency I think can be changed so we record maybe like TTFB latency for the console? That makes sense right?

You're right about EDGE and I was wrong. Placement is unpinned specifically so the worker runs at the colo nearest the client, so a developer reading the console sees the same edge their `nix build` hits. It only diverges for CI, and the label doesn't claim to speak for CI.

Let me check whether we can get the colo for free before designing anything.

content.text:
Pushed as `c276a7c`.

**Why staging said that:** my bug, from `c73bd3b`. Analytics Engine's type-conversion functions are `toUInt8` and `toUInt32` — **`toString` doesn't exist**. Every bucketed query wrapped its bucket in `toString`, so Cloudflare rejected the statement, the worker saw a non-200, and answered `storage_unavailable`. Every chart on staging has been dark since buckets shipped. The token and account id were fine.

The cast is gone; the bucket comes back as a JSON number and the row reader renders it.

**The lane could not have caught this**, and that's worth saying plainly: the stub accepts any statement, so it proves the worker composed what I intended, never that Cloudflare accepts it. The integration lane can't close the gap either — `/api/self/events` requires an admin and CI holds an OIDC token, which `require_admin` refuses by design. Reaching the real SQL API from a test needs a credential nothing in CI has.

**The message was also wrong**, which is worse than trash prose. It asserted a missing token to a deployment that had one. It now says what's true and points at `api.stats_query_failed`:

> **Counters unavailable** — Nothing is lost: reads, writes, and probes are still being counted. Check the worker log for `api.stats_query_failed`.

Favicon added — the capacitor on a dark tile, since a tab bar can be light or dark and a favicon inherits neither.

**On sweep fraction:** it's one of GC's three abort gates. If a collection decides to delete more than 25% of the inventory, it deletes nothing and reports the trip instead. It exists because the mark phase is the part that can be wrong — a bug that fails to mark live paths makes everything look dead, and the sweep would empty a cache every consumer trusts. A quarter of the store disappearing in one night is far more likely a bug than a real change in what's live. The cost is that a legitimate mass cleanup trips it and needs several runs to drain. Given the blast radius on the other side, I'd keep it.

Once staging redeploys on `c276a7c`, the charts should populate. If they still don't, the log line now names the upstream status and I'll chase that instead of guessing.

# ADR 0017: The collector refuses on blindness, not on scale

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-26
- **Context doc:** [0005-gc-on-the-cron.md](0005-gc-on-the-cron.md);
  [../security/threat-model.md](../security/threat-model.md)

## Context

The collector carried three abort gates. Two fire when it cannot see the
truth: an unreadable root narinfo or an unparseable lease means the mark
set is wrong, and a truncated enumeration means the inventory is
incomplete. The third fired on scale: a sweep whose candidate count
exceeded a quarter of the narinfo inventory aborted the run.

The third one cannot be satisfied. Aborting produces an empty deletion
plan, so nothing is deleted, so the next run enumerates the same
inventory and computes the same candidates and aborts again. The
candidate set only grows, because every path already past its grace
window stays past it. A deployment where more than a quarter of the cache
is genuinely dead stops collecting permanently, and the only exit is a
person with bucket access.

That is the wrong failure for this system twice over. A binary cache's
characteristic problem is unbounded growth, and this gate converts "a lot
is dead" into "nothing is ever collected". And the thing it protected
against is cheap here: over-deleting from a cache costs a rebuild and a
re-push, not data. The store paths still exist in every machine that
built them.

## Decision

1. The sweep fraction gate is removed, along with its constants, its
   `GateTrip` variant, and its report value.
2. The gates that remain are the ones that fire on blindness: an
   unreadable root narinfo, an unparseable lease, a truncated inventory
   or lease listing, an exhausted walk budget, and a corrupt generation
   document. Each of those means the collector's picture of what is live
   is incomplete, which is the condition worth refusing on.
3. How much one run may delete is not bounded.

## Consequences

A collection deletes everything the mark phase proved dead, however much
that is. A deployment that decommissions half its repositories collects
normally on the next tick instead of jamming.

The blast radius of a mark-phase bug widens: one that failed to mark live
paths would now sweep them. What limits it is unchanged and is the part
that was always doing the work: nothing is swept until its grace window
past the last lease that named it has passed, so a mistake needs to
survive fourteen days of nothing referencing a path. And the recovery is
a push, because that is what a cache is.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep the gate and add an override.** A variable an operator sets to let
one run through. Rejected: it makes the deadlock a thing you have to know
about and then know how to escape, and the escape is a setting nobody
reads until they are already stuck.

**Raise the fraction.** Any fixed fraction has the same deadlock at some
inventory, and picking a bigger number only moves the wall.

**Cap the deletions per run rather than refusing them.** Sweep at most N
and let successive runs drain the rest. This is a real option and would
bound a bug's damage per night while still converging. Rejected for now
because it adds a partial-sweep state to a collector whose runs are
currently whole, and the grace window already gives the same protection
in time rather than in count. Worth revisiting if a mark-phase bug ever
does happen.

**Why it was a gate:** ADR 0005 put it there as a blast-radius limit on a mark-phase bug. What's left fires on *blindness* rather than scale: unreadable root, unparseable lease, truncated inventory or lease listing, exhausted walk budget, corrupt generation. content.text:
Staging is already running `39c8e4`, so the gate is gone from the code — but `/api/self/health` reads the **last report**, and the last collection ran at 05:00 UTC today on the old build.

Two things can make it say `degraded`: the latest report has a `gate` set, or it finished more than 48 hours ago. With a daily cron the second is unlikely, so it's almost certainly the first — and I'd bet on the gate I just deleted, for a reason specific to staging:

`deploy.yml:65` pins `CACHET_DEPLOY_GC_GRACE_MS: "0"` on staging so the integration lane can sweep what it seeds. With grace zeroed, **every unleased path is a sweep candidate the moment it lands**. The integration lane pushes a path per run and deliberately can't renew a lease (it forces `GITHUB_REF` off the default branch), so staging's bucket is mostly dead paths. The candidate set has been way past a quarter of inventory for a long time, so the fraction gate tripped on essentially every run — which is also why staging has been accumulating rather than collecting.

So the gate wasn't hypothetical on staging; it was jamming it nightly.

It should clear itself at 05:00 UTC, when the collector next runs on `39c8e4` with no fraction gate, sweeps the backlog, and writes a report with `gate: null`. There's no way to trigger a deployed worker's cron by hand — Cloudflare only offers that in local dev — so it's a wait.

To confirm the cause rather than take my word:

```
curl -sS --netrc-file ~/.netrc https://cachet.staging.nox.so/api/self/health
```

If `gate` is `sweep_fraction_exceeded`, that's it and tomorrow fixes it. If it's `inventory_truncated`, `unreadable_root_narinfo`, or similar, it's a different problem and I'd want the run report. If `gate` is null and it still says degraded, then it's staleness and the collector hasn't completed in two days, which is its own thing worth chasing.
